deep.reconstruction:
The page is Gauss's catalogue of 'Tracte': plane curves that cross themselves transversally at double points ('vollständige Knoten'). A curve is recorded by the order in which its crossings are met along the curve. This is what is now called a Gauss word or Gauss code: each crossing letter occurs exactly twice. Points met only once are omitted.

(1) Normalisation and counting (implicit, mine). A word is written so that letters first appear in the order a, b, c, ... . The words are then listed lexicographically. The number of such words on n letters is the number of perfect matchings of 2n positions, (2n)!/(2^n n!) = (2n-1)!!. This gives 1, 3, 15, 105 for n = 1, 2, 3, 4. Gauss's lists have exactly these lengths: 1 (aa); 3 (aabb, abab, abba); 15; and 105 (Nos. 1-52 on this page, 53-105 on the next).

(2) Classification by stars, as stated in the header.
- '**': the word is impossible in itself, i.e. not even realisable as an open (non-closed) arc.
- '*': realisable as an open arc, but impossible once the curve must be closed without a new crossing point. The header wording is garbled ('Vorundmachsetzung eines neuen Knotenpunkts'), and this is my reading of the intended sense.
- No star: the word is realisable as a closed curve.

(3) Results by number of crossings.
- n = 2: abab is starred; aabb and abba are closed-realisable.
- n = 3: the unstarred words are 1 aabbcc, 3 aabccb, 7 abbacc, 9 abbcca, 10 abcabc (the trefoil diagram) and 15 abccba. The mark after 15 looks cancelled or faint; the next page confirms 15 is possible. Double stars: 5 abacbc and 13 abcbca. The rest have one star.
- n = 4 on this page: the unstarred words are 1, 3, 7, 9, 10, 15, 31, 33, 37, 39, 40, 45, 46, 48. These are exactly the members ≤52 of the list of 24 closed-realisable words given on the next page.

(4) Implicit criterion (mine, made explicit on the next page). Each star-free word satisfies Gauss's parity condition: between the two occurrences of any letter there is an even number of letters. Equivalently, if positions are numbered 0..2n-1, each letter occupies one even and one odd position. Every single-starred word I checked violates it:
- aabbcdcd: c at 4,6.
- aabcbddc: b at 2,4.
- abbcacdd: a at 0,4.
- abbcddac: a at 0,6.
- aabcddbc: b at 2,6.
- abcadbcd: b at 1,5.
So for n ≤ 4, '*' versus 'no star' is exactly parity failure versus parity success. The next page then states that parity is no longer sufficient from 5 crossings on (example abcadcedbe).

(5) Why a double star is justified, for 5 abacbc (argument mine).
- The sub-arc from the first a to the second a is a closed loop L1 through b.
- The sub-arc from the first c to the second c is a closed loop L2 through b.
- L1 does not contain c and L2 does not contain a. So L1 and L2 meet only at b, transversally.
- Two closed plane curves in general position meet an even number of times, so this is impossible even for an open arc.
- For abcbca this simple argument fails, because a corner of one loop lies on the other. Gauss's '**' there is plausible but not verified by me.

(6) Purpose. This is combinatorial 'Geometrie der Lage' (topology): deciding which crossing sequences can be drawn by a plane curve. It is the origin of the Gauss-code realisability problem.
errors: No genuine mathematical errors found on this page; the counts (1, 3, 15, 105) and the closed/not-closed classification agree with the parity criterion and with the next page's list of 24 realisable 4-crossing words.

The mark after No. 15 (abccba) looks like a cancelled or faint star. Correctly, abccba is realisable as a closed curve (nested kinks), and the next page counts it among the possible ones (105 and 15 are in the orbit 15.105.73.33).
The '**' assignments (impossible even as open arcs) are asserted without proof. I verified abacbc by an intersection-parity argument; the others I did not check exhaustively.
No. 14 has been overwritten (a correction of the numeral only).

results.what: Lexicographic enumeration of all double-occurrence words (Gauss words) with 1-4 crossings, numbering (2n-1)!! = 1, 3, 15, 105
results.modern_name: Gauss words/Gauss codes; count of perfect matchings, the double factorial (2n-1)!!
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Nachlass, published in Werke VIII); counting itself routine

results.what: Classification of words as realisable by a closed plane curve, by an open arc only, or not at all; for n ≤ 4 the closed-realisable ones are exactly those satisfying the even-interlacing (parity) condition
results.modern_name: Gauss's realisability problem for Gauss codes; Gauss's parity (evenness) condition
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (condition and the n=5 counterexample); full solutions by Nagy (1927), Dehn (1936), Read–Rosenstiehl (1976), Rosenstiehl, de Fraysseix–Ossona de Mendez

results.what: Distinction between realisability as an open arc ('Tract' without closure) and as a closed curve
results.modern_name: Realisability of Gauss words by immersed arcs versus immersed circles (plane curves / long curves)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss in this Nachlass; modern treatments in the theory of plane curves and virtual knots (e.g., Turaev on Gauss words)

deep.surprise_reason: This is Gauss's well-known Nachlass note 'Zur Geometrie der Lage, für zwei Raumdimensionen', published in Werke VIII. The parity condition and the Gauss-code realisability problem are standard attributions to Gauss in the knot-theory and graph-theory literature, so the page confirms known credit rather than revealing new results.
